facts.raw_span: A 75-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted with a prosthetic hip infection 10 days after revision surgery
chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 130–150 μmol/L)
hypertension, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and folate deficiency
drowsiness, confusion, disorientation, and hyperventilation
Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12
Temperature was 36.2°C
blood pressure 145/66 mmHg
pulse 80/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air
Sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 mmol/L, chloride 118 mmol/L, bicarbonate 5 mmol/L
Arterial blood gas: pH 7.18, pCO2 1.7 kPa, pO2 16.7 kPa, bicarbonate 8.3 mmol/L, base excess –22.7 mmol/L
corrected anion gap was 25 mmol/L
lactic acid 0.7 mmol/L, blood ketones <0.2 mmol/L, salicylate <0.4 mmol/L

concepts.why: The patient's arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.18, pCO2 of 1.7 kPa, and a corrected anion gap of 25 mmol/L, indicating a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, which is consistent with lactic acidosis.
The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes and presents with metabolic acidosis, which could be consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis, although the blood ketone level is not significantly elevated.

The patient is taking aspirin and presents with altered mental status and metabolic acidosis, which could be consistent with salicylate toxicity, although the salicylate level is not significantly elevated.
The patient has a history of prosthetic hip infection and presents with signs of systemic inflammation, including tachypnea and tachycardia, which could be consistent with sepsis.
The patient has a history of chronic kidney disease, which could contribute to the development of metabolic acidosis.
The patient is taking vancomycin and presents with signs of renal dysfunction, which could be consistent with vancomycin-induced nephrotoxicity.
The patient presents with hyperventilation and tachypnea, which could be consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome, although the oxygen saturation is normal.
The patient presents with signs of hypovolemia, including tachycardia and low blood pressure, which could be consistent with hypovolemic shock.
The patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12 and severe metabolic acidosis with a corrected anion gap of 25 mmol/L and low bicarbonate levels are indicative of metabolic acidosis.
